title: Pliers & Wrenches: Groove Joint Pliers, Open-End Wrenches, and Pipe Wrenches (This Old House)
summary: This This Old House short teaches practical hand-tool choices for common plumbing fasteners and emphasizes grip technique. It first contrasts groove joint (water pump) pliers with a wrench, showing how reversing the pliers changes their holding action and how to avoid stripping a nut. It then profiles combination wrenches and adjustable open-end wrenches for maximizing leverage and minimizing damage to hexagonal nuts. The segment concludes with pipe-wrench fundamentals on round pipe, including the head’s rocking action and the crucial three-point bite (three Corner bite) to prevent slipping and pipe damage. The lesson provides concrete, transferable tips for selecting the right tool and applying solid grip during loosening and tightening tasks.

sections.title: Pliers basics: groove joint pliers and reversing grip
sections.description: Introduces groove joint pliers and demonstrates how reversing the jaws can loosen or tighten a nut, noting that holding the pliers backwards may cause the jaws to open and slip, potentially stripping the nut if force is not applied correctly.

sections.title: Wrenches and leverage: selecting, adjusting, and avoiding damage
sections.description: Discusses different wrench types (combination wrench with fixed ends and open-end vs. adjustable open-end) and explains that an adjustable open-end wrench lets you apply more of your force with less risk of rounding or stripping a nut, while recognizing the role of grip strength when a pipe is involved.

sections.title: Pipe wrench mechanics and the three-point bite
sections.description: Explains the pipe wrench’s rocking head and tightening action on round surfaces, emphasizing the three-point bite (three Corner bite) where the wrench should contact the pipe at three points to avoid slipping and to protect the pipe threads from damage.

featured_techniques.technique: Backward orientation of groove joint pliers to facilitate loosening, then returning to a secure grip for turning
